title: Bhakti in the language of home
hookLine: a weaver, a tailor, a shopkeeper and a princess, all singing to God in the language of home
carry: bhakti: God hears love in any language
tomorrow: what did Ramana ask himself at sixteen?

lines: A WEAVER, A TAILOR, A SHOPKEEPER.
cards: A weaver at his loom in Varanasi, throwing the shuttle and singing. A tailor in Maharashtra with a needle in his hand and a name of God on his lips.
A shopkeeper whose ledgers of money owed to him, the story goes, ended up in the river. A princess in Rajasthan who sang that she had no one but Krishna.
A girl in a Tamil temple town who wore the garland meant for the god before it was offered. Faces from the weeks of the saints of bhakti.

teach.b: From the top of the year, look at who the tradition chose to remember. Kabir is remembered as a weaver. Namdev as a tailor.
Tukaram as a small trader whose business failed. Mirabai as a princess who walked away from palace rules. Andal as a girl raised by a temple gardener.
Looms, needles, ledgers, a palace, a garden. And notice what they sang in. Andal and the Nayanars sang in Tamil.
Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram in Marathi. Kabir, Surdas, Tulsidas and Mirabai in the spoken tongues of the north. In Bengal, the songs of Chaitanya's kirtan were made in Bengali.

teach.h: SUNG IN THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.
teach.b: The language of the kitchen and the market became a language of prayer. A song credited to Kabir lets God speak, in paraphrase: where are you looking for me?
I am right beside you. Not in the temple, not in the mosque, not in ritual and renunciation. Seek truly and you will find me in a moment.

teach.h: NO ONE ELSE BUT GIRIDHAR GOPAL.
teach.b: Mirabai, in paraphrase: my own is Giridhar Gopal, the cowherd who lifted the mountain, and no one else. Different saints, different gods named, different tongues.

teach.h: GOD HEARS LOVE IN ANY LANGUAGE.
teach.b: One shared teaching, and it is the heart of bhakti: God is reached by love, and love doesn't need the priest's language. Sanskrit stays sacred; it was never the only door.
That's why songs from those weeks are still sung by heart in kitchens, on pilgrim roads and in temple halls, in the language each family speaks.

how: The songs of the bhakti saints are sung in homes, temples and on pilgrim walks across India: Tukaram's abhangas, Kabir's dohas, Mirabai's bhajans and Andal's Tiruppavai, each in its own language.

o: loving devotion to God, sung in the language of home
a vow to leave home and live as a wandering monk
temple ritual done strictly by trained priests

games.q: the saints of bhakti — tap the pairs.
p: a princess who sang of Giridhar Gopal

s: the bhakti saints wrote only in Sanskrit
they sang in Tamil, Marathi, Bengali and the spoken tongues of the north.
Kabir sings that God is right beside the seeker
where are you looking for me, he asks: I am right beside you.
the saints are remembered mainly as temple officials
they're remembered as a weaver, a tailor, a trader, a princess, a gardener's daughter.

games.q: a seeker asks where to look for God: in the temple, on pilgrimage, or in rituals. what does Kabir's song say?
o: in the great temple, at the right hour.
on a long pilgrimage, far from home.
right beside you, if you truly seek.
games.why: the song turns the question around: not in temple or mosque or ritual, but right beside the seeker, found in a moment of true seeking.

practice: Find the language you first heard tenderness in, whatever it is.
If you pray, let one name of God in that language rest on the breath, again and again, the way the saints repeated a name; if you don't, choose a plain word for thanks in that same tongue.
Let it come and go with the breath, like a weaver's shuttle, back and forth.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Loving devotion, the saints' whole path, sung to God in the language of home.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: bhakti, loving devotion; the word for the saints' whole path.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti: God hears love in any language. Tomorrow, the modern teachers. That's today, done.
